newsitem.title: CHINA: No progress in S.Korea-China talks on defector.
newsitem.headline: No progress in S.Korea-China talks on defector.

text.p: South Korea and China had made no progress on Friday in resolving the deadlock on the fate of the most senior North Korean official who fled the hermit Stalinist state and sought shelter in Seoul's mission in Beijing.
"So far there is no progress," South Korean Embassy spokesman Chang Moon-ik said of the talks on Hwang Jang-yop, Pyongyang's top ideological theoretician.

Hwang walked into Seoul's mission in Beijing on February 12 and has been there ever since, surrounded by a Chinese security cordon of police with assault rifles, anti-riot trucks mounted with water cannon and armoured personnel carriers.
"We are still optimistic," said Chang, who has said that Hwang was not expected to leave China until after the end of February.
He hinted that the talks, stalled when China observed six days of mourning from last Thursday for the death of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, may again have been put on hold.
Channels were open with China's Foreign Ministry whenever necessary, Chang said when asked if negotiations on Hwang's fate were under way.
Chang declined to say what issues, if any, were holding up negotiations, and would not say if he would be allowed to leave next month.
"We want to bring Mr Hwang to (South) Korea, but we do not know when he will be able to come," Chang said.
Hwang's defection has entangled China in the enmity between Pyongyang and Seoul, forcing Beijing to choose between its old communist comrades and a new capitalist partner.
Beijing is apparently playing for time on the row in its backyard, unwilling to offend either of the two Koreas.
Analysts say China will in the end almost certainly allow Hwang, the architect of North Korea's governing ideology of strict self-reliance, to go to Seoul.
But Beijing wants to help its Stalinist neighbour save face by being seen to give Pyongyang's concerns due attention.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Tang Guoqiang called for calm on Thursday and said Beijing did not wish to see new tension on the Korean peninsula.

"We hope that all sides concerned seek with a calm and objective attitude a solution to appropriately resolve the matter to maintain peace and stability in the Korean peninsula," Tang told a news briefing.

"We do not wish to see this matter giving rise to new tensions in the Korean peninsula. Whether the problem is resolved fast or slow hinges completely on when and under what circumstances (the) concerned sides find a way to appropriately resolve it," he said.
Chinese police backed by armoured personnel carriers and a riot truck kept a tight guard around the Seoul mission, sealing off surrounding streets in the placid, tree-lined embassy district.
Vanloads of police also kept a close watch on Pyongyang's embassy a few kilometres (miles) away.

Hwang's defection threw extra strain on ties between the two Koreas -- still technically at war since their 1950-53 conflict ended only in a truce -- but there have been signs in recent days that the crisis may be easing.
Pyongyang, which at first insisted that Hwang had been kidnapped by South Korean agents, softened its stance last week by vowing to dismiss the ideologue if he had in fact defected.
